newsitem.title: UK: IPAI data foggy, but aluminium price seen climbing.
newsitem.headline: IPAI data foggy, but aluminium price seen climbing.

text.p: Latest stocks data from the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI), which showed a small rise, are difficult to interpret after Chinese stocks were excluded from the figures, analysts said.
But the unrelenting falls in LME inventories and tight stocks/consumption ratios support higher prices in the near-term, they added.

The institute, which started including data for China in its January figures, bowed after two months to vigorous criticism from analysts who complained of difficulties in tracking world production and stock trends after the changes.
The March stock figures which came out on Monday were the first to exclude China, but the previous month still included them.
"This just highlights the confusion...the data will remain tainted as long as they report the January and February data with the Chinese figures," said analyst Angus MacMillan of broker Billiton.
"This implies that the rise is larger than the 10,000 tonnes which has been stated," he added.
IPAI data showed unwrought aluminium inventories increasing by the end of March to 1.562 million tonnes from 1.552 million in February, when the Chinese figures were still being included.
Total stocks rose by 19,000 tonnes to 3.096 million from 3.077 million during the same period.
In any case, the fall in LME stocks since March strengthens the bullish case for aluminium, analysts said.
"It is important to look at the overall picture," said analyst Nick Moore of Flemings Global Mining Group.
Combined LME and producer stocks fell by 224,000 tonnes in the first quarter and, since March, LME stocks have fallen by about 75,000 tonnes.
The stocks/consumption ratio is down to 7.8 weeks, only about a week away from the seven-week level that Moore regards as critical.
"As the aluminium market crosses the Rubicon...we would expect to see more jockeying in the market," he said.
Even though not all the stock reductions were going into consumption, an increase in consignment stocks showed that investors were putting their faith in rising prices, Moore added.

Broker GNI said in a report ahead of the release of IPAI data: "While there are always cynics (including ourselves) when stocks fall, conspiracy theorists should be careful when it occurs for a long period of time -- stock demand or a shortage of supply are usually the main reason."
MacMillan agreed falling stocks would support higher prices in the short term, but he was cautious about the second half of the year.
"The $64,000 question is whether the LME stock falls can be maintained as we enter the summer," he said.
A combination of seasonal weak demand, restarts of mothballed production and the build-up to full output of new operations could put a damper on the market.
MacMillan is forecasting a surplus in the second half of the year after a deficit in the first half, bringing the market into rough balance for the year.
